title: Health and Safety at Work Act & risk assessment
blurb: Who is legally responsible for safety at work, how risk assessment works, and what you do when you spot a hazard.
question: On a busy morning you find a box of stock left in the corridor outside the decontamination room, a wet patch on the floor, and a first aid box with no plasters left. A trainee says it's the practice manager's job, not yours. What does health and safety law actually expect of you?

teach.h: One Act, two sets of duties
teach.body: The Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 (HASAWA) is the main UK health and safety law. It puts duties on employers AND on employees. Employers must protect the health, safety and welfare of staff and anyone else affected, such as patients and visitors, 'so far as is reasonably practicable'. That means balancing the risk against the time, cost and effort of controlling it. The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) enforces the Act and can inspect, issue notices and prosecute.

rows.label: Main duty
values: Take reasonable care of yourself and others

rows.label: Policy
values: Know it and work to it

rows.label: Safety kit
values: Never misuse or interfere with it

teach.caption: Employee duties come from sections 7 and 8 of the Act: take reasonable care, co-operate with your employer, and don't interfere with anything provided for safety.

teach.body: A hazard is anything with the potential to cause harm: a wet floor, a used scalpel, a bottle of disinfectant. A risk is the chance that the hazard actually causes harm, and how bad that harm could be. The Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999 require employers to make a 'suitable and sufficient' assessment of risks, and to write down the significant findings if they employ five or more people. Inspectors expect to see these assessments.

steps.label: Identify the hazards
steps.sub: Walk round, check records, ask staff

steps.label: Decide who might be harmed and how

steps.sub: Write down significant findings and act on them

teach.h: Everyday hazards in a dental practice
head: Hazard
Who's at risk
Typical control
teach.caption: Most slips and trips are prevented by good housekeeping: clear corridors and fire routes, prompt clean-up of spills, and no trailing cables.

teach.h: You spot a new hazard: what to do
items: Identify it: notice what could cause harm and who is near it.
Make it safe if you can do so without putting yourself at risk: move the box to storage, isolate the spill and warn others.
Report it to the practice manager or health and safety lead.
Record it if your practice requires it (incident log or accident book).
Review the controls so it doesn't happen again.

teach.h: First aid and the paperwork you'll see
teach.body: The Health and Safety (First-Aid) Regulations 1981 require adequate first aid equipment and people, at minimum an appointed person to take charge. The first aid box must be checked regularly and restocked. If items are missing, report it so it is refilled: don't take supplies from the emergency drugs kit, and never keep tablets or medicines in the first aid box. Practices also display the HSE 'Health and safety law' poster (or give staff the leaflet) and an employers' liability insurance certificate.

teach.h: The four kinds of safety sign
teach.caption: Safety signs follow the Health and Safety (Safety Signs and Signals) Regulations 1996. The colour and shape tell you the message before you read the words.

teach.text: Health and safety is NOT only the employer's job. You have a legal duty to take reasonable care and to co-operate. Walking past a hazard you could easily make safe, or rushing and skipping routine checks, is how most practice incidents happen.

items: HASAWA 1974: employers protect everyone 'so far as is reasonably practicable'; employees take reasonable care and co-operate.
Hazard = potential to harm. Risk = likelihood and severity of that harm.
Risk assessment in five steps: identify, who and how, evaluate and control, record and implement, review.
New hazard: identify, make safe if you can, report, record, review.
First aid box checked and restocked regularly; report missing items.

summary: You can now explain the duties HASAWA 1974 places on employers and on you, tell a hazard from a risk, walk through HSE's five steps to risk assessment, and respond correctly when you find a hazard or an empty first aid box.

A.q: A box of impression material has been left in the middle of a corridor. What is the best immediate action?
options: Put a cone beside it until it is collected
Ask reception to warn people about it
Move it safely to its storage area
Push it against the wall for now
A.why: If you can make a hazard safe without risk to yourself, you should. Moving the box to proper storage removes the trip hazard completely.

whyNot.0: A cone warns people but leaves the hazard in place when it could simply be removed.
whyNot.1: Warnings rely on people remembering; removing the obstruction is the better control.
whyNot.3: A box against the wall can still trip people and may narrow a fire escape route.

A.q: Under HASAWA 1974, which of these is a legal duty of an EMPLOYEE?
options: Take reasonable care of themselves and others
Write the practice health and safety policy
Arrange the employers' liability insurance
Carry out and record the practice fire risk assessment
A.why: Section 7 of HASAWA requires employees to take reasonable care of their own and others' health and safety, and to co-operate with the employer.

whyNot.1: Writing the safety policy is the employer's duty (required with five or more employees).
whyNot.2: Employers' liability insurance is an employer's legal requirement.
whyNot.3: The fire risk assessment is the duty of the 'responsible person', usually the employer.

A.q: Which statement best describes a RISK, as opposed to a hazard?
options: Anything that could possibly cause harm
A substance listed on a safety data sheet
A written record of the practice's health and safety rules
The chance that harm occurs, and how severe it is
A.why: A hazard is something with the potential to cause harm; the risk is the likelihood of that harm happening and its severity.

whyNot.0: That is the definition of a hazard, not a risk.
whyNot.1: A hazardous substance is a hazard; the risk depends on how it is used and controlled.
whyNot.2: That describes a policy or procedure, not a risk.

B.q: You notice a wet patch on the floor outside the decontamination room. What should you do?
options: Mop it after the current patient leaves
Lay paper towels on it and carry on
Report it to the manager and leave it
Clean or isolate it and warn others
B.why: A wet floor is an immediate slip hazard. Clean it up or isolate it, and warn others until it is safe.

whyNot.0: Delaying leaves the hazard in place while people walk through it.
whyNot.1: Paper towels can become slippery and don't warn anyone.
whyNot.2: Reporting is good, but you should also make it safe if you can.

B.q: Which is the correct order for HSE's five steps to risk assessment?
options: Identify hazards, who is harmed, evaluate, record, review
Evaluate, identify hazards, record, who is harmed, review
Record, identify hazards, evaluate, review, who is harmed
Identify hazards, record, evaluate, review, who is harmed
B.why: Identify the hazards, decide who might be harmed and how, evaluate the risks and decide on precautions, record and implement, then review.

whyNot.1: You can't evaluate a risk before identifying the hazard.
whyNot.2: You record findings after evaluating them, not before you have identified anything.
whyNot.3: Deciding who might be harmed comes second, not last, and recording follows evaluation.

B.q: During a check you find the first aid box is missing several items. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Take what's needed from the emergency drugs kit
Remove the box until someone restocks it
Report it so the box is restocked promptly
Wait for the next scheduled annual check
B.why: First aid provision must be checked and restocked regularly. Report the shortfall so it is refilled quickly.

whyNot.0: The emergency drugs kit is for medical emergencies and must stay complete.
whyNot.1: Removing the box leaves no first aid provision at all.
whyNot.3: An incomplete box could be needed today; waiting is not acceptable.

C.q: Which regulations specifically require employers to carry out a 'suitable and sufficient' risk assessment?
options: The Health and Safety (First-Aid) Regulations 1981
The Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999
The Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998
The Reporting of Injuries, Diseases and Dangerous Occurrences Regulations 2013
C.why: The Management Regulations 1999 require a suitable and sufficient risk assessment, with significant findings recorded where there are five or more employees.

whyNot.0: The First-Aid Regulations cover first aid equipment and personnel.
whyNot.2: PUWER covers the safety of work equipment.
whyNot.3: RIDDOR covers reporting certain incidents to HSE.

C.q: The practice is fully booked and staff are hurrying between rooms. Which behaviour most increases the chance of an accident?
options: Reporting hazards as soon as seen
Following the cleaning schedule
Rushing and skipping routine checks
Keeping corridors free of boxes
C.why: Rushing and bypassing routine checks is a leading cause of workplace incidents.

whyNot.1: Cleaning schedules help prevent slips and infection.
whyNot.3: Clear corridors prevent trips and keep escape routes open.

C.q: Which body enforces the Health and Safety at Work Act in a dental practice?
options: The General Dental Council
The Information Commissioner's Office
The British Dental Association
The Health and Safety Executive
C.why: HSE (and local authorities for some premises) enforces health and safety law, with powers to inspect, issue notices and prosecute.

whyNot.0: The GDC regulates dental professionals, not workplace health and safety law.
whyNot.1: The ICO enforces data protection law.
whyNot.2: The BDA is a professional association and trade union; it has no enforcement role.

reteach.title: Safety is a team sport
reteach.question: Think of the practice like a football team: the manager sets the tactics and provides the kit, but every player still has to play their part. Who is responsible for what?

blocks.body: Your employer is the manager: they write the game plan (the safety policy and risk assessments), buy the kit (PPE, safe equipment), and train the team. You are a player: you follow the plan, wear the kit, look out for team-mates and shout when you see danger. If a player ignores a hazard on the pitch, the team loses, however good the plan was.

Reporting an empty first aid box

explain.body: HASAWA 1974 makes the employer protect everyone 'so far as is reasonably practicable': safe equipment, safe systems, training, a written policy (5+ staff) and free safety kit. Employees must take reasonable care of themselves and others, co-operate, and not misuse anything provided for safety.

test.q: Which of these is the employer's duty rather than the employee's?
options: Wearing the gloves provided
Providing PPE free of charge
Reporting a frayed cable
Co-operating with safety rules
test.why: Employers must provide required safety equipment and can't charge staff for it.

whyNot.0: Wearing PPE provided is the employee's duty.
whyNot.2: Reporting faults is part of the employee's duty to co-operate and take care.
whyNot.3: Co-operation is an employee duty under section 7.

explain.body: A hazard is the thing that could cause harm. Risk is how likely that harm is and how serious it would be. A bottle of disinfectant locked in a cupboard is still a hazard, but the risk is low. The same bottle unlabelled on a worktop is a much higher risk.

test.q: A used scalpel blade on the bracket table is best described as:
options: A risk
A control measure
A hazard
A dangerous occurrence
test.why: The blade has the potential to cause harm, so it is a hazard. The risk is the chance someone is cut.

whyNot.0: Risk is the likelihood and severity of harm, not the object itself.
whyNot.1: A control measure reduces risk, such as a safer sharps system.
whyNot.3: A dangerous occurrence is a specific RIDDOR category of incident.

explain.body: Identify the hazards; decide who might be harmed and how; evaluate the risks and decide on precautions; record the significant findings and implement them; review and update. Review whenever something changes, such as new equipment, new staff or after an incident.

letters.word: Who could be harmed, and how

test.q: When should a practice review a risk assessment?
options: Only when the HSE requests it
Only when a patient complains
Whenever something significant changes
Only at the end of every five-year period
test.why: Risk assessments should be reviewed regularly and whenever something changes, such as new equipment, staff or an incident.

whyNot.0: Waiting for HSE would leave risks unmanaged.
whyNot.1: Complaints may prompt a review, but they aren't the only trigger.
whyNot.3: A fixed five-year gap is far too long; changes must trigger a review.

explain.h: Responding to hazards and first aid
explain.body: When you find a hazard: identify it, make it safe if you can without risk, report it, record it if required, and review the controls. The first aid box is checked and restocked regularly. Report missing items; never raid the emergency drugs kit or keep medicines in the first aid box.

test.q: You notice a trailing cable across the floor by the dental chair. What comes FIRST?
options: Record it in the accident book
Make it safe if you can do so safely
Email the practice manager later
Review the practice risk assessment
test.why: After identifying a hazard, make it safe straight away if you can do so without risk, then report it.

whyNot.0: Recording comes after the hazard has been made safe.
whyNot.2: Delaying leaves the trip hazard in place.
whyNot.3: Reviewing controls is the final step, not the first.
